Risso's dolphins (Grampus griseus) exhibit a suite of life-history characteristics typical of slow-reproducing, long-lived odontocetes. Parturition results in a single neonate, with newborns measuring approximately 130 cm [Lb = approximately 130 cm] in length at birth, a value that places them among the larger-bodied delphinid calves. This substantial size at birth is complemented by a corresponding neonatal wet weight of about 20,000 grams [Wwb = about 20,000 grams], representing a considerable maternal investment that is likely linked to the species' deep-diving foraging ecology, as a larger, more robust calf is better equipped for rapid post-natal development. The energetic costs associated with gestation and lactation are significant for adult females, who must maintain a stable core body temperature of roughly 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C] throughout these demanding physiological processes. Data from stranding records and captive observations indicate that the maximum recorded lifespan for this species is approximately 42.5 years [am = approximately 42.5 years], though individuals in the wild may face higher mortality rates from fisheries interactions and predation, potentially shortening this theoretic at a temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C]al upper limit.

The reproductive biology of Grampus griseus is characterized by a notably lengthy gestation period, which field studies have estimated to last for roughly 412 days [tg = roughly 412 days] at a maternal body temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C]. This protracted gestation, lasting well over a year, is consistent with the development of a highly precocial calf capable of swimming and diving almost immediately following the birth event. The extended in utero development is also reflected in the length at puberty; males typically reach sexual maturity when they have attained a body length of approximately 270 cm [Lp = approximately 270 cm], which often falls within a documented range of 2.6 to 2.8 m. This body size threshold is correlated with significant social and behavioral changes, as males begin to compete for access to females in a complex social structure dominated by stable, multi-male alliances, which are thought to be crucial for reproductive success.

Following the birth of a calf, the mother-calf bond is intense and prolonged, typical of many social cetaceans. The time from birth to weaning is estimated to be around 458 days [tx = around 458 days] at a body temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], a period during which the calf transitions from a diet of milk to solid prey, primarily cephalopods. This prolonged period of nutritional dependence is energetically costly for the mother and is a major factor influencing the species' reproductive output. Females produce a single calf per calving event [N_R_i = single calf per calving event], and the calving interval of approximately 2.4 years corresponds to a reproductive frequency of roughly 0.4 calves per year [Ri = roughly 0.4 calves per year]. This low reproductive rate underscores the high investment placed into each individual offspring and makes the population particularly vulnerable to external pressures such as bycatch and habitat degradation.

Growth parameters for female Risso's dolphins indicate that they achieve their ultimate or asymptotic length later in life, with the maximum recorded body length for females reaching up to 400 cm [Li = up to 400 cm]. The time since birth at which female calves attain sexual maturity is reported to be approximately 9 years [tp = approximately 9 years], with measurements taken at a consistent core body temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C]. In contrast, male calves require a longer developmental period before reaching puberty, with the time since birth at puberty for males being around 11 years [tp = around 11 years], also at the same internal body temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C]. This sex-specific difference in maturation rates is common among polygynous or promiscuous mammals and is often linked to the delayed competitive ability required for males to successfully secure mating opportunities within the fluid social alliances that characterize this species.

Adult females, having reached their ultimate length, can attain an ultimate wet weight of as much as 425,000 grams [Wwi = 425,000 grams], with a typical range reported in the literature falling between 300 and 500 kilograms (300-500 kilograms) [Wwi = 300-500 kilograms]. This substantial mass enables the species to sustain the energetic demands of repeated gestation and deep-diving foraging, an adaptation that complements the species' slower life-history strategy, with a reproductive output limited to a single calf per event [N_R_i = single calf per event] and a frequency of approximately 0.4 calves per year [Ri = approximately 0.4 calves per year], reflecting an adaptive response to the unpredictable availability of their deep-sea squid prey. This ecological specialization places a premium on adult survival and offspring quality over high fecundity. Consequently, any disruption to adult survival rates, whether from direct mortality or from chronic stress and ocean noise that impairs foraging efficiency, can have disproportionately severe consequences for population persistence, as the low reproductive output cannot quickly compensate for even modest increases in adult mortality.
